title: Heatwaves are consuming the resistance reserve in temporary propping
excerpt: On 9 October 2026 Ground Engineering published an industry view by Vicky Mastoridou of Groundforce Shorco on thermal loading and soil volatility in temporary works. Record heatwaves in 2026 mean temporary propping and shoring schemes are operating beyond the climatic envelopes assumed at design. Desiccation and cracking in clays such as London Clay, followed by rapid rainfall, can alter ground parameters and cause lateral earth pressures to rise faster than conventional models anticipate. Simultaneously, restrained steel props, sheet piles and bracing convert solar heating into additional compressive axial forces, consuming part of the structural resistance calculated for earth pressure alone.
linkedinReady:
Heatwaves are no longer an anomaly on UK sites. They are changing the loads your temporary works were designed for.

On 9 October 2026 Ground Engineering published an industry view by Vicky Mastoridou of Groundforce Shorco examining thermal loading and soil volatility in temporary works. Sustained temperatures over 30°C, desiccation and cracking of clay soils such as London Clay, and the rapid rainfall that follows can alter the ground parameters assumed at design. Lateral earth pressures behind retaining structures can spike faster than conventional models anticipate.

At the same time, restrained steel props, sheet piles and bracing absorb solar radiation. Because they cannot expand freely between walls, walers and slabs, thermal energy converts into additional compressive axial forces. A prop sized for earth pressure alone can see part of its resistance reserve consumed by thermal load. The practical outcome can be denser or higher-capacity propping, with consequences for working space and access.

BS 5975-1:2024 sets out the temporary works procedure as industry good practice. The design brief and the temporary works register need to capture the expected climatic envelope and the trigger for review if that envelope is exceeded. Distinguishing thermal load spikes from actual ground movement (through load-cell data and competent inspection) becomes part of the control process. A change in weather conditions that affects the assumptions in the brief is worth sending back for review before the works simply continue.

Standard does not automatically mean low risk when the weather envelope has changed.

Educational only. Not for construction. Subject to the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 9 October 2026 Ground Engineering published an industry view by Vicky Mastoridou (CEng, MICE), development manager at Groundforce Shorco, titled Redefining geotechnical limits: thermal loading and soil volatility in temporary works. The piece notes that the summer of 2026 again surpassed previous temperature benchmarks, with sustained thermal loads over 30°C, widespread desiccation and shifting water tables no longer treatable as short-term weather anomalies. In clay-rich formations such as London Clay, extended dry spells can shrink and crack the ground, altering stiffness and strength. Subsequent intense rainfall can penetrate those cracks rapidly, causing localised softening, swelling and pore-water pressure changes. Lateral earth pressures behind retaining structures can therefore rise faster than conventional design models anticipate. For temporary works this means ground parameters assumed at design may not remain valid through construction. At the same time, exposed structural steelwork (hydraulic props, sheet piling, bracing frames) absorbs solar radiation, raising surface temperatures above ambient. Because these members are restrained between retaining walls, walers and slabs they cannot expand freely; thermal energy converts into additional compressive axial forces. A strut specified to resist active earth pressure must simultaneously resist geotechnical thrust and its own restrained thermal expansion, consuming part of the structural resistance calculated under partial factors. The practical consequence can be a requirement for stronger, larger or denser propping layouts, reducing working clearance. Distinguishing actual ground movement from thermal load spikes requires careful interpretation of load-cell data.

Temporary works are not a short-lived exception to the duty to plan, manage and monitor construction work. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase and requires contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for a temporary works procedure; it is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. When the climatic envelope assumed in the design brief is exceeded, the ground parameters, earth pressures and thermal loads that justified the scheme, the inspection frequency and the monitoring regime may no longer hold. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. A proprietary propping or shoring system whose published capacity was calculated for a defined set of ground and temperature conditions is not low risk if the actual conditions have already moved outside that envelope and the brief has not been revisited. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: State the expected climatic envelope (temperature range, duration of exposure, rainfall after dry periods) and the trigger for formal review if that envelope is exceeded in the design brief and on the temporary works register entry.
When heatwave conditions, desiccation or rapid rainfall occur, treat the change as a potential alteration to the temporary works assumptions. Send it back for review before the works simply continue.
Where load cells or other instrumentation are installed, record both load and temperature so thermal spikes can be distinguished from ground movement. Do not rely on a visual check alone.
Confirm that the person inspecting has the competence and authority required by the project procedure to interpret changes in load or ground conditions.
If denser or higher-capacity propping is required to accommodate thermal load, confirm that working space, access and plant movements remain acceptable under the revised arrangement.
At the point of removal or alteration, confirm that the permanent structure (or the next temporary state) is ready to take the load under the current ground and temperature conditions.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: Educational briefing only. Not for construction. Based on the Ground Engineering industry view of 9 October 2026 and publicly available HSE temporary works guidance. It is not a design, a check or a statement that any particular temporary works arrangement is adequate or inadequate under elevated temperatures or changed ground conditions. No loads, capacities, temperatures or soil parameters have been calculated here. Subject to project-specific verification and acceptance under the project temporary works procedure. AI-assisted drafting requires competent review before use on site.
